issues.legal_issue: A land transfer made after the statutory cutoff is included in calculating a holder’s landholding unless it satisfies an applicable exception, even when it is said to implement an earlier family arrangement.
material_facts: The holder executed a registered gift of land to his adult unmarried daughter after the statutory cutoff.
He asserted that the gift implemented an earlier family arrangement intended to provide for his daughter, but did not prove that arrangement or explain the delay in executing the gift.

The authorities found that the transfer was not proved to be in good faith and appeared designed to defeat the ceiling law; the holder and his sons remained in possession and enjoyed the land’s income.
issues.conclusion: The gifted land had to be included in calculating the holder’s total landholding because the transfer was not shown to fall within an exception.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(6) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960 requires a post-cutoff transfer to be ignored in determining the ceiling area unless it falls within an exception in the proviso. The relevant exception requires proof of good faith, adequate consideration and an irrevocable instrument, and excludes benami transfers and transfers for the immediate or deferred benefit of the holder or the holder’s family.

rule.if: ceiling_area_determination and post_cutoff_land_transfer and not qualifying_protected_transfer

predicates.ceiling_area_determination: The proceeding determines the landholding to be used in calculating a landholder’s ceiling area.
predicates.post_cutoff_land_transfer: The landholder transferred land after the applicable statutory cutoff.
predicates.qualifying_protected_transfer: The transfer was proved to be in good faith, for adequate consideration, under an irrevocable instrument, not benami, and not for the immediate or deferred benefit of the landholder or the landholder’s family.

issues.definition: When a ceiling-area determination concerns a post-cutoff land transfer that does not qualify for protection, the transferred land is included in the landholder’s holding.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings about a land transfer cannot be reopened in an appeal under Article 136 when those findings have been accepted by the High Court.
material_facts: The prescribed authority and appellate authority found that the holder had not proved that the gift was in good faith and was not intended for the benefit of the holder or his family.
The High Court affirmed those findings, and the matter reached the Supreme Court by special leave under Article 136.
issues.conclusion: The correctness of the concurrent factual finding could not be canvassed in the appeal under Article 136.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the accepted concurrent finding as a finding of fact whose correctness could not be challenged in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal under Article 136 following the grant of special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_finding_accepted_by_h: The lower authorities made the same factual finding and the High Court accepted it.

issues.definition: In an Article 136 appeal, a concurrent factual finding accepted by the High Court is not reopened.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional validity of a land-ceiling provision protected by Article 31-B cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates Article 31-A.
material_facts: The holder challenged the provision governing post-cutoff transfers as inconsistent with Article 31-A.
The Act and its relevant amendments had been included in the Ninth Schedule.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge could not succeed because Article 31-B immunised the provision from that challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31-A and 31-B of the Constitution apply; Article 31-B protects a law included in the Ninth Schedule from the asserted constitutional challenge. The Court relied on D.G. Mahajan v. Maharashtra, [1977] 2 SCR 790, and Ambika Prasad v. U.P. State, [1980] 3 SCR 1159.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a land-ceiling law.
predicates.challenged_law_in_ninth_schedule: The challenged law has been included in the constitutional schedule that gives it immunity from the asserted challenge.

issues.definition: A constitutional challenge to a land-ceiling law included in the protected schedule does not succeed on the asserted ground.

issues.legal_issue: Excluding an adult unmarried daughter from the statutory definition of a landholder’s family does not, by itself, establish unconstitutional discrimination between women and men.
material_facts: The statutory definition included minor daughters but excluded adult daughters, including adult unmarried daughters, from a landholder’s family.
The holder argued that this distinction discriminated against adult unmarried daughters compared with adult unmarried sons.

The provision did not take property from a daughter or give property to a son; the scheme allowed a holder with a propertyless adult son to retain additional land, without giving the son a right to that land.
issues.conclusion: The provisions did not discriminate between men and women as such, and the challenge under Article 14 failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require the Court to extend an additional land-retention allowance to a holder because an adult unmarried daughter exists where the legislation does not take her property or confer property on a comparable son. The Court relied on Ambika Prasad v. U.P. State, [1980] 3 SCR 1159, which had concluded that the scheme did not create tangible sex discrimination.

predicates.article_14_equality_challenge: The proceeding challenges a statutory family definition as discriminatory on grounds of sex.
predicates.adult_daughters_excluded_from_family_def: The statutory scheme excludes adult daughters from the family unit used for calculating a landholder’s ceiling area.
predicates.no_property_taken_from_daughter_or_confe: The scheme neither takes property from a daughter that it leaves with a son nor grants the son a right to land retained by the holder.

issues.definition: An equality challenge based on the exclusion of adult daughters does not succeed where the scheme neither takes their property nor confers property on sons.
